title: Ramadan: the mosque

cards: Late one night in Ramadan, the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, goes out to the mosque in Madinah and prays. A few men see him and pray behind him.
The next night, more people come, and the next, more again, until the mosque is full of people waiting for him. 'A'ishah tells it in Sahih al-Bukhari. Then, one night, he doesn't come out. They wait.
He stays home. At the dawn prayer, he explains why.

teach.h: HE STAYED HOME, OUT OF MERCY.
teach.b: His explanation, in paraphrase: your being there was not hidden from me, but I was afraid this prayer would be made obligatory on you, and you wouldn't be able to keep it up.
He stayed home out of mercy, to keep a voluntary prayer voluntary. The night prayer of Ramadan began as a gift, and he protected it from becoming a burden.
Al-Bukhari also reports that later, in the time of 'Umar, he walked into the mosque one Ramadan night and found people praying scattered, some alone, some in small groups behind one man.
He gathered them into one congregation behind a single reciter, Ubayy ibn Ka'b. Another night he saw them praying together and said, in paraphrase, what a fine new thing this is.
That gathered night prayer came to be called tarawih, which you first met in year one. Schools differ on how long it should be, and not every community prays it in congregation.
Shia Muslims, for example, keep Ramadan nights with their own prayers. Before the prayer, the food.
In a hadith in al-Tirmidhi, whoever gives a fasting person food to break the fast has a reward like theirs, without the fasting person's reward being reduced at all.

So some mosques open their doors at sunset: long sheets on the floor, volunteers carrying trays, dates, water, soup, rice, strangers passing plates to strangers. The family table seats the people who share your house.
The mosque table seats whoever walks in: the student far from home, the new neighbor, the person who would otherwise break the fast alone.

how: In Ramadan, mosques may hold a congregational night prayer called tarawih, which reports in al-Bukhari trace to 'Umar gathering people behind one reciter, and some host iftars at sunset open to anyone, following a hadith in al-Tirmidhi on the reward of feeding a fasting person; Shia Muslims keep Ramadan nights with their own prayers.

o: a month when only the imam fasts on the people's behalf
the fasting month, with night prayer and open iftar tables
the night prayer Muslims pray once a year in a mosque

games.q: the mosque in Ramadan — tap the pairs.
p: so the prayer wouldn't become obligatory

s: the Prophet stopped coming out because too few people came
the mosque was filling up; he feared the prayer would be made obligatory on them.
'Umar found people praying in scattered groups and gathered them behind one reciter
al-Bukhari keeps the report; the reciter was Ubayy ibn Ka'b.
feeding a fasting person takes away from that person's reward
in al-Tirmidhi, the one who feeds gets a reward like theirs, without theirs being reduced.

games.q: you're 'Umar. you walk into the mosque on a Ramadan night and find people praying in scattered groups, each with its own leader. what do you do?
o: gather them into one congregation behind a single reciter.
games.why: he gathered them behind Ubayy ibn Ka'b, and later, seeing them praying together, called it a fine new thing.

practice: Picture a long cloth on a mosque floor at sunset, plates going down the line, and someone you don't know beside you, passing you a date.

Then think whether a mosque near you holds an iftar open to guests, or, if you don't go to a mosque, of one person who eats alone and how you might share a meal. If you pray, you can remember the people who cook and serve.

wordCard.voice: Ramadan. The month of fasting, kept in the mosque with the night prayer called tarawih and with iftars where whoever walks in gets fed. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: the name given to the gathered night prayer of Ramadan.

carryVoice: Your line: the community table. Whoever walks in gets fed. Rest well.
